chapters.1: A wisdom psalm contrasting two paths in life. The person who delights in God's law is like a healthy tree planted by water, bearing fruit and thriving, while the wicked are like chaff blown away by the wind, with no lasting stability or future.
chapters.2: A royal/messianic psalm about rebellious nations plotting against God and his chosen king. God laughs at their defiance and installs his king on Zion, warning earthly rulers to submit and find safety by trusting him rather than opposing him.
chapters.3: A morning prayer of trust written while surrounded by enemies, traditionally linked to David fleeing Absalom. Despite being outnumbered, the psalmist says he can still sleep peacefully because God is his shield and will answer when he calls.
chapters.4: An evening prayer of trust spoken to people chasing empty, false things instead of God. The psalmist urges them to stop and reflect quietly, then testifies that God has given him more joy than any harvest, letting him sleep in safety.
chapters.5: A morning prayer asking God to hear a cry for help against deceitful, wicked people. The psalmist contrasts God's hatred of lies and violence with his own hope to worship in God's house, asking to be led safely while his enemies face the consequences of their own schemes.
chapters.6: A penitential psalm of someone physically and emotionally crushed, perhaps by illness, pleading for mercy rather than punishment. Amid nightly weeping, the mood shifts at the end to confidence that God has heard and will deal with his tormentors.
chapters.7: A cry for vindication from a man falsely accused, who insists on his own innocence and asks God to judge fairly between him and his enemies. He pictures the wicked as hunters who end up falling into the very traps they set for others.
chapters.8: A hymn of praise marveling at God's glory displayed in the night sky, and then at the surprising dignity God has given human beings. Though small compared to the heavens, humanity has been crowned with honor and given care over the rest of creation.
chapters.9: A psalm of praise and confidence after God has judged hostile nations and defended the psalmist's cause. He celebrates that God is a refuge for the oppressed and the poor, then asks God to keep acting that way against those who still oppose him.
chapters.10: A cry asking why God seems distant while the wicked prey on the poor and act as though God doesn't notice or care. The psalm ends with renewed confidence that God does see the suffering of the vulnerable and will act as their defender.
chapters.11: A psalm of trust answering friends who urge the psalmist to flee danger. He refuses, insisting that God sees everything from his heavenly throne and will deal with the wicked, while the upright will see his face.
chapters.12: A lament over a society where honesty has broken down and people flatter and lie to each other while the vilest rise to the top. God responds with a promise to protect the poor and needy, and his pure words are trusted as reliable even when human words are not.
chapters.13: A short, intense lament asking how long God will seem to forget the psalmist while sorrow and a triumphant enemy wear him down. It turns at the end into trust and a resolve to sing, even before relief has fully arrived.
chapters.14: A psalm describing human corruption in blunt terms: those who live as if there is no God, and none who truly seeks him. It closes with a longing for God to rescue his people and restore their fortunes.
chapters.15: A wisdom psalm asking who is fit to be in close fellowship with God, and answering with a list of character traits: honesty, keeping one's word, not slandering or exploiting others, and refusing bribes and unfair profit.
chapters.16: A psalm of trust and contentment in which the psalmist says God alone is his treasure and security, better than any other pursuit. He expresses confidence that God will not abandon him even in death, but will show him the path of life and lasting joy.
chapters.17: A plea for a fair hearing from someone confident of his own integrity, asking God to test his heart and find no wrong in him. He asks to be guarded like the pupil of an eye from enemies who are like prowling lions, and ends hoping to see God's face.
chapters.18: A long thanksgiving song celebrating a dramatic rescue from deadly danger, picturing God coming down in storm, earthquake, and fire to save his servant. The king recounts God's strength working through him in battle and closes praising God as his unshakable rock.
chapters.19: A psalm in two parts: first praising how the skies silently proclaim God's glory every day, then praising God's law as perfect, trustworthy, and more valuable than gold. It ends with a prayer that the psalmist's words and thoughts would please God.
chapters.20: A short prayer for a king going into battle, asking God to answer him, send help, and grant his requests. The people declare their trust is in God's name rather than in military strength like chariots and horses.
chapters.21: A royal psalm of thanksgiving celebrating the blessings God has given the king, including victory, long life, and glory. It also anticipates God's judgment on the king's enemies, closing with praise for God's strength.
chapters.22: A psalm that begins in deep anguish, with the psalmist feeling abandoned by God while surrounded by mockers and violent enemies who mistreat him in vivid, almost unbearable detail. Partway through it turns dramatically to praise, as the psalmist anticipates that God will be glorified before the whole world.
chapters.23: A psalm of trust picturing God as a shepherd who provides rest, guidance, and protection even through danger and death's shadow. The psalmist ends confident that God's goodness will follow him and that he will always have a place with God.
chapters.24: A psalm declaring that the whole earth belongs to God, then asking who may approach his holy presence, answering: those with clean hands and a pure heart. It closes with a vivid call for the gates to open as the mighty King of glory enters.
chapters.25: A prayer for guidance and forgiveness from someone surrounded by enemies and burdened by past sin. The psalmist asks God to teach him God's ways, remember his mercy rather than old failures, and ultimately rescue him from trouble and shame.
chapters.26: A psalm of self-examination in which the psalmist asks God to test his integrity, pointing out that he has avoided the company of liars and wicked people and stayed devoted to worship. He closes asking not to be swept away with sinners, affirming his resolve to keep walking uprightly.
chapters.27: A psalm of confidence opening with bold trust that God is light and salvation against any enemy, then shifting to a deep longing simply to be near God's presence. It ends with an exhortation to wait courageously for the LORD even when feeling abandoned.
chapters.28: A cry for help from someone afraid of being grouped with the wicked and swept into their fate, asking God to repay evildoers for their hidden cruelty. It turns to praise once the psalmist feels assured that God has heard, closing with a prayer for God to shepherd his people.
chapters.29: A hymn of praise picturing God's voice in a violent storm, breaking cedars and shaking the wilderness with overwhelming power. The psalm moves from this display of strength to a quiet closing prayer that God would give his people strength and peace.
chapters.30: A thanksgiving psalm for recovery from a near-fatal crisis, praising God for turning mourning into dancing. The psalmist reflects on a season of false security followed by distress, concluding that God's favor, though sometimes hidden, always returns.
chapters.31: A prayer for rescue from both enemies and personal distress, moving through vivid grief, isolation, and slander before settling into trust. The psalmist famously commits his spirit into God's hands and closes urging others to take courage in God's faithfulness.
chapters.32: A psalm of relief after confessing sin, describing the physical misery of hidden guilt and the freedom that came once the psalmist admitted it openly. It closes with an invitation to trust God rather than being stubborn like an unruly animal, and to rejoice in forgiveness.
chapters.33: A call to praise God with music for his trustworthy word and his power in creating the world by simply speaking. It reminds the hearers that no army or strength saves anyone, only God's watchful care over those who trust him.
chapters.34: A thanksgiving psalm inviting others to taste and see that God is good, based on the psalmist's own experience of being delivered from trouble. It turns into practical wisdom for a good life, promising that God is especially near the brokenhearted.
chapters.35: An urgent plea for God to fight on the psalmist's behalf against enemies who repay his kindness with hostility and false accusations. He recalls mourning for them when they were in trouble, and asks that those who now mock his suffering be put to shame.
chapters.36: A psalm contrasting the wicked, who have no fear of God and plot evil even in bed, with God's vast, reliable love reaching to the heavens. It closes with a prayer to keep walking in that love and a note that evildoers eventually fall.
chapters.37: A wisdom psalm urging patience instead of envy toward the wicked, since their apparent success is short-lived like grass that withers. It repeatedly promises that those who trust and wait on God will inherit the land, while evildoers fade away.
chapters.38: A penitential psalm describing the psalmist's sin-related physical and emotional collapse, including wounds, exhaustion, and abandonment by friends. He openly confesses his guilt and ends begging God not to be far away while enemies close in.
chapters.39: A meditation on human frailty and the shortness of life, written by someone who tried to stay silent about his suffering but finally spoke out. He asks God to show him how fleeting his days are and to have mercy before he passes from this life.
chapters.40: A psalm combining thanksgiving for a past rescue with a renewed cry for help in present trouble. The psalmist recalls God lifting him from a pit and says obedience matters more than ritual sacrifice, then asks for quick deliverance despite feeling poor and needy.
chapters.41: A psalm that begins by blessing those who care for the poor, then turns personal as the psalmist, sick and betrayed by a close friend, asks God for healing and mercy. It ends confident that God's continued support proves his favor, despite enemies wishing for his death.
chapters.42: A psalm of deep longing, comparing the thirst for God to a deer panting for water, written by someone who misses worshiping with others and is taunted for his faith. He repeatedly questions his own despair and coaches himself back toward hope in God.
chapters.43: A short continuation of the same longing as Psalm 42, asking God to vindicate the psalmist against an unjust nation and to send light and truth to guide him back to worship. It ends with the same refrain urging his downcast soul to put its hope in God.
chapters.44: A communal lament recalling how God once gave Israel's ancestors victory, then asking why God now seems to have abandoned the nation to defeat and humiliation despite their faithfulness. It closes with an urgent plea for God to wake up and act on their behalf.
chapters.45: A royal wedding psalm praising a king's beauty, justice, and victorious reign, then addressing his bride and urging her to devote herself fully to him. It closes promising that the king's name and line will be remembered and honored for generations.
chapters.46: A psalm of trust declaring God a refuge and strength even if the earth itself were shaken, pointing to a peaceful city protected by God's presence amid worldwide chaos. Its famous center calls listeners to "be still" and recognize God as God over all nations.
chapters.47: A short, energetic call to all peoples to clap and shout in celebration of God as the great King over the whole earth. It pictures God ascending to his throne amid trumpet blasts, ruling over every nation.
chapters.48: A hymn celebrating Jerusalem (Zion) as a beautiful, secure city because God dwells there, recalling how enemy kings were struck with fear and fled at the sight of it. It invites worshipers to walk around the city and pass on its story to future generations.
chapters.49: A wisdom psalm addressed to everyone, rich and poor alike, pointing out that wealth cannot buy anyone out of death and that even the richest end up like everyone else in the grave. It contrasts this with confidence that God will personally redeem the psalmist's life from death.
chapters.50: A psalm picturing God as judge, summoning all people and declaring that he doesn't need animal sacrifices since everything already belongs to him. He calls for sincere thanksgiving and obedience instead, and sharply rebukes the wicked for their hypocrisy and sin.
chapters.51: A deeply personal penitential psalm, traditionally David's prayer after his sin with Bathsheba, pleading for mercy and thorough cleansing from guilt. He asks God to create a clean heart within him, insisting that genuine repentance matters more to God than any ritual sacrifice.
chapters.52: A short rebuke of a boastful, deceitful person who trusts in wealth and cruelty rather than in God. The psalmist contrasts this with his own security, comparing himself to a flourishing olive tree planted in God's house.
chapters.53: A psalm nearly identical to Psalm 14, describing widespread human corruption and the absence of anyone who truly seeks God. It closes with a longing for God to rescue and restore his people.
chapters.54: A brief cry for help against hostile attackers who show no regard for God, asking God to save and vindicate the psalmist by his own name and strength. It ends in confident thanksgiving once deliverance from trouble is anticipated.
chapters.55: A lament over betrayal by a trusted friend, mixed with terror at violent threats in the city, leading the psalmist to wish he could simply fly away and escape. He settles into praying regularly through the day and famously counsels casting one's burdens on God.
chapters.56: A prayer for help from someone surrounded by enemies who twist his words and watch his every move, who nonetheless keeps repeating that he will trust rather than fear. He notes with comfort that God keeps track of his tears and ends resolved to walk confidently before God.
chapters.57: A cry for mercy from someone hiding from danger, comparing his enemies to lions with spear-like teeth while he takes refuge under God's wings. The mood shifts to resolved praise, with the psalmist determined to sing at dawn and declare God's glory among the nations.
chapters.58: An indictment of corrupt judges and leaders who are wicked from birth, compared to venomous snakes immune to any charm. The psalmist asks God to disarm and remove them so that people will see justice is real and God does judge the earth.
chapters.59: A night-time cry for protection from violent enemies who prowl the city like snarling dogs, insisting he has done nothing to deserve their hostility. He resolves to keep singing of God's strength as his defense, confident that God will deal with them in his own time.
chapters.60: A communal lament after a military setback, asking why God seems to have rejected his people and left the land shaken. It moves to a reminder of God's past promises over various territories, concluding that human help is worthless but God can still give victory.
chapters.61: A short prayer from someone far away and overwhelmed, asking God to lead him to a secure, rock-like refuge he cannot reach on his own. It includes a prayer for the king's long life and ends with a vow to keep praising God daily.
chapters.62: A psalm of calm trust declaring that God alone is a secure rock while enemies plot to bring the psalmist down with flattery and lies. It warns against putting confidence in wealth, power, or oppression, since only God can truly be relied on.
chapters.63: An intense expression of longing for God's presence, comparing spiritual thirst to physical thirst in a dry, barren land. The psalmist recalls past experiences of God's goodness and says he will keep praising God even while enemies who seek his life will come to ruin.
chapters.64: A prayer for protection from secret plots and slander, where enemies shoot cutting words like hidden archers. The psalmist trusts that God will suddenly turn their own schemes against them, leaving the righteous to rejoice.
chapters.65: A joyful hymn of praise for answered prayer and forgiven sin, moving into awe at God's power over mountains and seas. It closes with a rich picture of God's generosity in nature, watering the earth so abundantly that the hills and valleys seem to sing for joy.
chapters.66: A call for the whole earth to praise God for his awesome deeds, recalling how he brought Israel through the sea and later tested them like silver in fire. The psalmist personally testifies that God heard his prayer because he came to him with a sincere heart.
chapters.67: A brief prayer asking God to bless his people so that his ways become known throughout the earth. It calls all nations to praise and rejoice in God's just rule, trusting that blessing on the people will overflow into blessing for the whole world.
chapters.68: A triumphant hymn picturing God marching ahead of his people like a warrior, scattering enemies and caring for the fatherless, widows, and the lonely. It recalls past victories from the wilderness journey to Sinai and calls all kingdoms of the earth to sing praises to God's strength.
chapters.69: An intense cry for rescue from someone who feels he is drowning in deep water, hated and mocked for his devotion to God. He asks God to punish his persecutors harshly, then turns to praise, confident that God hears the poor and will restore Zion.
chapters.70: A brief, urgent plea for God to hurry and help someone who is poor and needy and under attack from enemies. It mirrors Psalm 40's closing verses, asking that those who seek to harm him be shamed while those who seek God rejoice.
chapters.71: A prayer of trust from someone praying across a lifetime, from youth into old age, asking God not to abandon him now that he is aging and weak. He vows to keep declaring God's righteous acts to the next generation despite enemies who claim God has forsaken him.
chapters.72: A royal psalm, framed as a prayer for the king, asking that he rule with justice especially for the poor and needy, and that his reign bring lasting peace and prosperity. It envisions his influence spreading worldwide, with all nations eventually blessing his name.
chapters.73: A wisdom psalm wrestling with envy toward the wicked, who seem to prosper carefree while the righteous struggle, until the psalmist gains perspective in God's sanctuary and sees their sudden downfall ahead. He concludes that nearness to God, not worldly success, is truly good.
chapters.74: A communal lament after the destruction of the temple, crying out as enemies have burned God's sanctuary and mocked his name. The psalmist recalls God's ancient power over creation and chaos, pleading for him to remember his covenant people and act again.
chapters.75: A psalm of thanksgiving in which God himself speaks, promising to judge fairly and warning the arrogant not to boast, since he alone decides who rises and falls. It pictures a cup of judgment that the wicked will have to drink to its dregs.
chapters.76: A hymn celebrating God's awesome power displayed in defending his people, where enemy chariots and horses were struck still in their tracks. It calls all who witness such judgment to stand in reverent fear and bring their offerings to the God who humbles rulers.
chapters.77: A psalm moving from sleepless, anguished questioning about whether God's mercy has run out, to a deliberate choice to remember God's past wonders instead. The psalmist recalls God's power at the sea and leading Israel like a shepherd, finding comfort in history rather than present feelings.
chapters.78: A long historical psalm retelling Israel's story from the exodus through the wilderness to King David, as a lesson for future generations. It repeatedly shows a pattern of God's provision and patience met with the people's forgetfulness and rebellion, ending with God's choice of David as shepherd-king.
chapters.79: A lament over the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, describing the dead left unburied and the nation mocked by surrounding peoples. The psalmist pleads for mercy rather than punishment for old sins, and for God to act for the sake of his own reputation among the nations.
chapters.80: A lament pleading for God, pictured as Israel's shepherd, to restore a nation that feels abandoned and overrun. It uses the image of a vine that God once planted and made flourish but has now left exposed to be trampled and devoured, repeatedly begging for restoration.
chapters.81: A festival psalm calling Israel to celebrate with music, then shifting into God's own voice recalling how he rescued them from Egypt and gave them his law. It laments that the people refused to listen and imagines how much better things could have gone had they stayed faithful.
chapters.82: A short, striking psalm in which God rebukes unjust judges and rulers for favoring the wicked instead of defending the poor and fatherless. Despite their position of authority, God declares that they are still mortal and will be judged like anyone else.
chapters.83: An urgent appeal for God to act against a coalition of surrounding nations plotting to wipe out Israel entirely. The psalmist asks God to defeat them as decisively as he did famous enemies in Israel's past, so that they will recognize God as supreme over all the earth.
chapters.84: A psalm expressing deep longing and joy at the thought of being in God's house, comparing it to how even sparrows find a safe home there. It declares that one day worshiping God is worth more than a thousand elsewhere, closing with a blessing on those who trust him.
chapters.85: A prayer recalling how God once forgave and restored his people, now asking him to do so again after a season of displeasure. It closes with a beautiful vision of mercy, truth, righteousness, and peace coming together to bring blessing back to the land.
chapters.86: A personal prayer from someone who calls himself poor and needy, appealing to God's mercy and uniqueness among all so-called gods. He asks for an undivided heart to fear God's name and for a visible sign of God's help against proud, violent opponents.
chapters.87: A short celebration of Zion as God's beloved city, imagining people from many foreign nations, even old rivals, being counted as born there. It closes picturing singers and dancers declaring that all their life springs from this city God has established.
chapters.88: The bleakest of the psalms, a relentless cry from someone who feels he is already among the dead, abandoned by friends and overwhelmed by God's wrath, with no resolution or turn to praise at the end. It stands as an honest voice for despair that keeps crying out even without an answer yet.
chapters.89: A psalm that begins celebrating God's covenant promise to give David's line an everlasting throne, praising God's might over creation. It then turns into painful lament, as the psalmist asks why God seems to have rejected and humiliated the very king he promised to establish forever.
chapters.90: A meditation on human mortality attributed to Moses, contrasting God's eternity with how quickly human life passes like grass or a dream. It asks God to teach wisdom through this awareness of limited days and to show favor that outweighs past hardship.
chapters.91: A psalm of trust describing the safety of someone who takes refuge in God, pictured as shelter under wings and protection from disaster, disease, and danger day and night. It closes with God's own promise to rescue, protect, and give long life to the one who loves and knows him.
chapters.92: A song for the Sabbath giving thanks for God's works and reflecting on how the wicked flourish only briefly like grass before perishing. It compares the righteous instead to palm trees and cedars that stay fruitful even in old age.
chapters.93: A brief, majestic hymn declaring that the LORD reigns, robed in strength, more powerful than the roar of mighty floods and seas. It closes affirming that God's decrees are completely trustworthy and his holiness endures forever.
chapters.94: A cry for God, the judge of the earth, to act against wicked rulers who oppress widows, foreigners, and the fatherless while assuming God doesn't notice. The psalmist finds comfort in God's discipline and defense, trusting he will ultimately turn the wicked's own evil back on them.
chapters.95: An invitation to worship God joyfully as creator and shepherd, followed by a solemn warning not to harden one's heart as Israel's ancestors did in the wilderness. It uses that history as a caution to listen and respond to God today rather than testing him.
chapters.96: A call for all the earth to sing a new song to God, declaring his greatness above all other so-called gods and inviting every nation to bring offerings and worship. It pictures all of creation, heavens, sea, and fields, rejoicing because God is coming to judge the world in righteousness.
chapters.97: A hymn proclaiming that the LORD reigns, surrounded by awe-inspiring displays of fire and lightning that melt mountains and put idol-worshipers to shame. It ends assuring the righteous that light and gladness are reserved for those who love God.
chapters.98: A joyful call to sing a new song because God has worked a visible victory and shown his faithfulness to all nations. It invites instruments, voices, and even the sea and hills to join in celebrating God as the coming judge of the world.
chapters.99: A hymn proclaiming God's holy, reigning authority, recalling how leaders like Moses, Aaron, and Samuel called on him and were answered even while held accountable for wrongdoing. It repeatedly calls worshipers to exalt God because he is holy.
chapters.100: A short, joyful call to worship inviting all the earth to serve God with gladness and enter his presence with thanksgiving. It grounds that joy in the simple truths that God made his people and that his love and faithfulness never end.
chapters.101: A royal psalm in which the psalmist commits to personal integrity and to surrounding himself only with honest, faithful people. He vows to keep deceitful and slanderous people out of his house and to deal firmly with wrongdoing in the land he leads.
chapters.102: A lament from someone who feels physically wasted away, lonely as a desert bird, and worn down by God's displeasure, written with an eye toward future generations. It turns to confidence that God will yet restore Zion, contrasting human frailty with God's unchanging eternity.
chapters.103: A rich psalm of praise listing specific benefits God gives: forgiveness, healing, rescue, and compassion like a father's for his children. It compares human life to grass that withers but insists God's love for those who honor him lasts forever.
chapters.104: A nature hymn praising God as the one who designed the whole created world, from stretching out the sky to setting boundaries for the seas. It moves through mountains, animals, and seasons as evidence of God's wisdom and provision, closing with a wish that sin would vanish from the earth.
chapters.105: A historical psalm celebrating God's faithfulness to Israel from Abraham's covenant through Joseph's rise in Egypt to the exodus plagues and the gift of the promised land. It frames the whole story as reason to give thanks and remember God's wonders.
chapters.106: A historical psalm confessing Israel's repeated failures, from grumbling after the exodus to idol worship and injustice in the land, despite God's many rescues. It ends asking God to gather and save his people again in spite of this long record of unfaithfulness.
chapters.107: A thanksgiving psalm telling four different stories of people in distress, lost wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and storm-tossed sailors, who all cried to God and were rescued. Its refrain repeatedly urges people to praise God for his goodness and wonderful works.
chapters.108: A psalm of confident praise combining pieces of earlier psalms, vowing to sing to God among the nations and recalling his promises over various territories. It closes admitting human help is useless while trusting God to give victory.
chapters.109: An intense imprecatory psalm cursing a false accuser and betrayer with a long list of disasters for him and his family. It shifts at the end to the psalmist's own weakness and poverty, asking God to help him personally so his enemies will know God is behind it.
chapters.110: A royal/messianic psalm in which God addresses the king directly, inviting him to a position of honor and promising to make his enemies his footstool. It also declares him a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, pointing to a king who is both ruler and priest.
chapters.111: A short hymn praising God's great works, his faithfulness to his covenant, and his provision for his people. It closes with a saying also found in Proverbs, that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
chapters.112: A wisdom psalm describing the blessings of the person who fears God and delights in doing what is right, including generosity, stability, and a steady heart that doesn't fear bad news. It contrasts this security with the frustrated anger of the wicked who watch it happen.
chapters.113: A short hymn praising God's name from sunrise to sunset, marveling that though he is exalted far above the heavens, he stoops down to lift the poor from the dust. It closes with the image of God giving a childless woman a home full of children.
chapters.114: A brief, vivid psalm recalling the exodus, personifying the sea and the Jordan River as fleeing and the mountains as skipping like startled animals at God's presence. It calls all the earth to tremble before the God who can turn rock into flowing water.
chapters.115: A psalm contrasting the living God, who acts as he pleases, with lifeless idols that have mouths, eyes, and ears but cannot speak, see, or hear. It calls Israel and all who fear God to trust him instead, promising ongoing blessing to those who do.
chapters.116: A personal thanksgiving from someone who faced death and cried out to God, who answered and preserved him. He resolves to keep serving God publicly, famously noting that God values the lives of his faithful ones, and vows to pay his vows before the whole community.
chapters.117: The shortest psalm, a brief two-verse call for all nations to praise God simply because his kindness toward his people is great and his truth lasts forever.
chapters.118: A thanksgiving psalm celebrating deliverance from surrounding enemies, declaring it is better to trust God than to rely on people or rulers. It contains the well-known image of a rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, and celebrates the day God has made as one for rejoicing.
chapters.119: The longest psalm by far, an extended, acrostic meditation praising God's law, word, and commandments as a source of life, wisdom, and comfort through affliction and persecution. Across many short stanzas it repeatedly expresses love for God's word and a plea for help to keep living by it.
chapters.120: A short lament from someone living among hostile, war-loving people, worn out by their lying speech. He longs for peace even though those around him seem to always want conflict.
chapters.121: A well-loved psalm of trust, the first of the "songs of ascents," picturing the psalmist looking to the hills and affirming that his real help comes from God, maker of heaven and earth. It reassures that God never sleeps and will watch over every step, now and always.
chapters.122: A joyful pilgrimage psalm expressing gladness about going up to Jerusalem to worship, describing the city as a center of justice and gathering for the tribes. It closes with a well-known call to pray for the peace of Jerusalem.
chapters.123: A brief, humble psalm comparing the psalmist's dependence on God to a servant watching for a signal from their master. It pleads for mercy after enduring contempt and scorn from the proud.
chapters.124: A short thanksgiving psalm celebrating a narrow escape from overwhelming danger, picturing it as nearly being swallowed or drowned. It credits the rescue entirely to God and compares the deliverance to a bird escaping a snare.
chapters.125: A psalm of trust comparing those who trust God to the unshakeable mountains surrounding Jerusalem. It asks God to do good to the upright while reassuring that the wicked will not ultimately dominate the righteous.
chapters.126: A joyful psalm remembering a past restoration from captivity that felt like a dream, followed by a prayer for a similar restoration now. It closes with the hopeful image of someone sowing in tears but later reaping with joy.
chapters.127: A wisdom psalm insisting that human effort to build a house, guard a city, or secure the future is useless without God's involvement. It also celebrates children as a blessing and reward from God, like arrows in a warrior's hand.
chapters.128: A wisdom psalm describing the blessings awaiting the person who honors God, including satisfying work, a flourishing family, and living to see one's grandchildren. It ties personal happiness to the wider well-being of Jerusalem and Israel.
chapters.129: A psalm recalling Israel's long history of being attacked and afflicted yet never ultimately overcome, comparing its enemies to grass on a rooftop that withers before it can be harvested. It closes hoping those who hate Zion will go unblessed.
chapters.130: A penitential psalm crying out from a place of deep distress, famously described as crying "out of the depths." It finds hope not in personal innocence but in God's forgiveness, urging patient waiting the way a watchman waits for dawn.
chapters.131: A short psalm of humble trust in which the psalmist says he has stopped striving over things too great for him, resting instead like a contented weaned child with its mother. It closes urging Israel to hope in God with that same quiet trust.
chapters.132: A psalm recalling David's devotion in seeking a resting place for God's presence (the ark) and God's reciprocal promise to establish David's line and dwell in Zion. It closes with blessings on Zion's priests, the poor, and the king's enduring line.
chapters.133: A very short psalm comparing the goodness of family or community unity to fragrant oil poured out and to refreshing dew on the mountains. It frames unity itself as a place where God's blessing flows.
chapters.134: The shortest psalm but one, a brief call for temple servants who keep watch at night to lift their hands and bless God, closing with a blessing pronounced back on them from Zion.
chapters.135: A hymn of praise recounting God's choice of Israel and his mighty acts in nature, in Egypt's plagues, and in conquering other kings for Israel's benefit. It contrasts God's living power with the powerless idols worshiped by other nations.
chapters.136: A hymn of thanksgiving built on a repeated refrain, "his mercy endures forever," listing God's creative power and his acts in Israel's history, from the exodus to the conquest of kings. The refrain after every line turns the recitation itself into an act of worship.
chapters.137: A raw lament written from exile in Babylon, recalling captors mocking the exiles by demanding songs of Zion while they weep by the river. It ends with an intensely bitter cry for vengeance against Babylon for what it did to Jerusalem.
chapters.138: A thanksgiving psalm for answered prayer, promising to praise God publicly and noting that he pays attention to the lowly even though he is exalted above all. It closes confident that God will keep protecting the psalmist and complete what he has started in him.
chapters.139: A meditation on God's total, intimate knowledge of the psalmist, who cannot go anywhere, even the furthest heights or depths, beyond God's presence. It moves into wonder at being carefully formed in the womb, then asks God to search his heart and lead him in the right way.
chapters.140: A prayer for protection from violent, deceitful people who set traps and speak venomous words, likely referring to slanderous plots against the psalmist. It expresses confidence that God defends the poor and the righteous even while asking for the attackers' schemes to backfire on them.
chapters.141: An evening prayer asking that it rise before God like incense, with a specific request for self-control over his own speech and actions. He welcomes correction from the righteous but asks for protection from the schemes and traps of the wicked.
chapters.142: A cry of complaint from someone who feels utterly alone, with no one to care for him and enemies setting hidden traps. He calls God his only refuge and asks to be freed from this trapped, imprisoned feeling so he can praise God again among others.
chapters.143: A penitential plea for mercy from someone pursued and crushed by enemies, feeling as hopeless as the long dead. He asks God to teach him to do God's will and lead him in the right path, trusting God's righteousness rather than his own.
chapters.144: A royal prayer thanking God for military strength and skill, then marveling that God bothers with mortal, short-lived humans at all. It asks for rescue from deceitful foreign enemies and closes picturing a nation blessed with prosperity, strong families, and peace.
chapters.145: An alphabetic hymn of praise celebrating God's greatness, compassion, and faithfulness toward everyone and everything he has made. It highlights that God is near to all who call on him sincerely and lists the many ways he cares for the needy and upholds the fallen.
chapters.146: A hymn warning against putting ultimate trust in human rulers, who are mortal and limited, and instead praising God who defends the oppressed, feeds the hungry, and cares for strangers, orphans, and widows. It closes declaring that God will reign forever.
chapters.147: A hymn praising God for both grand and tender acts, from naming every star to healing the brokenhearted and feeding young ravens. It highlights that God delights not in human strength but in those who humbly trust him, and closes celebrating his unique care for Israel.
chapters.148: A sweeping call for all creation, angels, sun, moon, stars, weather, mountains, animals, and every kind of person, to praise God together. It grounds this universal praise in the fact that God created and sustains everything by his command.
chapters.149: A joyful call to praise God with music and dancing because he delights in his people and gives them victory. It closes with a more martial image of God's people carrying out judgment, reflecting a time when praise and battle for God's cause were closely linked.
chapters.150: The final psalm and a grand closing doxology, calling for praise with every instrument available, trumpet, harp, dance, cymbals, and more. It ends with the simplest and broadest invitation in the whole book: let everything that has breath praise the LORD.
